content.description: In 1905 and 1915, Einstein changed our idea of space, time and gravity. And without his calculations, your GPS would be off by several kilometers.

hero.hook: Time is not one universal clock. And gravity is not an invisible rope.

blocks.text: In **1905** and **1915**, **Albert Einstein** published two theories that turned physics upside down. Until then, science mostly followed [[Newton]]: time flowed the same way for everyone, everywhere.

Einstein showed that space and time are linked, and that gravity can be understood as a curving of that fabric. These ideas explain [[black holes]] and the [[Big Bang]]. They also correct the GPS in your phone, every single day.

**Special relativity** rests on two simple ideas. The laws of nature are the same for everyone moving at a constant speed. And the speed of light in a vacuum, **about 300,000 km/s**, is the same for everyone, whether you race toward the light or away from it.

blocks.caption: Albert Einstein, author of the theory of relativity

blocks.text: For light to always keep the same speed, time has to give. This is [[time dilation]]: the faster an object moves, the more slowly time passes for it compared with someone at rest. It is not an illusion. **Atomic clocks**, instruments that measure time with extreme precision, have measured it.

From this Einstein also drew [[E=mc²]]: mass is a very concentrated form of energy. Because **c**, the speed of light, is enormous, a tiny amount of mass can release colossal energy. That is one pillar of [[nuclear physics]], the study of atomic nuclei and their reactions.
In 1905, Einstein was not a university professor. He worked as an examiner at the patent office in Bern, Switzerland.

Ten years later, Einstein published **general relativity**. Newton saw gravity as an invisible force pulling masses toward each other. Einstein offered another picture: **spacetime**, space and time joined into a single fabric, behaves like a flexible sheet.

A heavy mass, like the Sun, dents that sheet. Picture a bowling ball on a trampoline. A marble rolled past it does not travel straight: it follows the dip. In the same way, the Earth orbits because it follows the curve the Sun creates.

Even light follows those curves. In **1919**, the British astronomer **Arthur Eddington** checked it during an eclipse: the apparent positions of stars behind the Sun were slightly shifted. Einstein became famous overnight.

GPS satellites circle at about **14,000 km/h**, some **20,000 km** up. To place you within a meter, their clocks have to stay in step with clocks on the ground. But two relativistic effects are at work at once.

Because of their speed, time up there runs a little more slowly, an effect of special relativity: roughly **7 microseconds** lost per day. Because gravity is weaker at that altitude, time up there runs a little faster, an effect of general relativity: roughly **45 microseconds** gained.
Without relativistic corrections, the position error of a GPS could reach about **11 km** a day.
The net result is a gain of about **38 microseconds** a day. That sounds minuscule. At the speed of light, it is already enormous for navigation.

sections.title: GPS, the proof in your pocket

blocks.text: General relativity predicts black holes: regions where the curvature is so strong that not even light gets out. Einstein doubted they really existed. Both [[radio astronomy]], the study of the sky in radio waves, and recent images have since confirmed them.

In **1916**, he also predicted **gravitational waves**: ripples in spacetime made by cosmic catastrophes, such as two black holes merging. Detecting them took until **2015** and the **LIGO** observatory, a ground-based detector sensitive to the shivering of space itself.

Finally, these equations opened the way to an expanding universe, the basis of the Big Bang model. Einstein had first added a **cosmological constant**, a mathematical term to force the universe to stand still. Hubble's observations later convinced him otherwise.
**E=mc²** ties mass to energy. General relativity says that gravity curves spacetime. Without those corrections, your GPS would be off by several kilometers every day.

Big Bang.explanation: Cosmological model describing the origin and evolution of the Universe from a phase of extreme density and temperature.

E=mc².explanation: Equivalence between mass and energy: a small mass corresponds to an enormous energy, amplified by the square of the speed of light (300,000 km/s). This is the principle behind the atomic bomb and nuclear energy.

Newton.explanation: English physicist (1643-1727) who formulated the law of universal gravitation, seeing gravity as a force of attraction between masses.

Time dilation.explanation: Time runs more slowly for an object moving fast or sitting in a strong gravitational field. GPS satellites correct for this shift of 45 microseconds a day; without the correction, their accuracy would drift by 11 km a day.

black holes.explanation: Celestial objects so dense that their gravitational field prevents any form of matter or radiation from escaping.

nuclear physics.explanation: Branch of physics studying the nucleus of atoms and the resulting reactions, based on mass-energy equivalence (E=mc²).

radio astronomy.explanation: Branch of astronomy that studies celestial bodies by observing the radio waves they emit.

time dilation.explanation: Time runs more slowly for an object moving fast or sitting in a strong gravitational field. GPS satellites correct for this shift of 45 microseconds a day; without the correction, their accuracy would drift by 11 km a day.

quiz.explanation: Special relativity is based on two ideas: the laws of nature are the same for any observer at a constant speed, and the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for everyone.
options: The laws of nature are the same for any observer at a constant speed, and the speed of light is the same for everyone
Gravity does not exist and time is completely frozen
Space is infinite but time stops at each star
Light travels faster depending on the direction of movement
quiz.question: On what two ideas is special relativity, published in 1905, based?

quiz.explanation: In 1905, Einstein was not a university professor: he worked as an examiner at the patent office in Bern, Switzerland.
options: True
False
quiz.question: True or false: in 1905, when he published special relativity, Einstein was already a recognized university professor.

quiz.explanation: Time dilation means that the faster an object moves, the slower time passes for it compared to someone at rest, an effect measured by atomic clocks.
options: The faster an object goes, the slower time passes for it compared to an observer at rest.
Time stops completely beyond a certain speed
Time only slows down in the vacuum of space
Time speeds up for any moving object
quiz.question: What does time dilation describe?

quiz.explanation: E=mc² shows that mass is a very concentrated form of energy: a very small mass can release colossal energy.
options: Mass is a highly concentrated form of energy
Energy can never be transformed into mass
The speed of light varies depending on the mass of the object
Only kinetic energy counts in physics
quiz.question: What does the formula E=mc² mean?

quiz.explanation: Einstein proposed that gravity is a curvature of space-time: a mass like the Sun hollows this fabric, and objects follow this curvature.
options: Like a curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass
Like an invisible force transmitted instantly
Like a magnetic field produced by the stars
Like a simple constant acceleration
quiz.question: How does general relativity describe gravity?

quiz.explanation: In 1919, Arthur Eddington observed during an eclipse that the apparent position of stars behind the Sun was shifted, confirming Einstein's theory.
options: British astronomer Arthur Eddington
Physicist Enrico Fermi
Astronomer Frank Drake
Physicist Stephen Hawking
quiz.question: Who verified in 1919, during an eclipse, that light is deflected by the Sun's gravity?

quiz.explanation: Without relativistic corrections, the GPS position error could reach around 11 km per day.
quiz.question: Without relativistic corrections, how many kilometers per day could GPS be wrong?

quiz.explanation: The speed effect slows the clocks by about 7 microseconds per day, while the gravity effect advances them by about 45 microseconds: the net result is an advance of about 38 microseconds per day.
options: True
False
quiz.question: True or false: Once the two relativistic effects are combined, the clocks on GPS satellites advance about 38 microseconds per day compared to those on the ground.

quiz.explanation: We had to wait until 2015 and the LIGO observatory to detect the gravitational waves predicted by Einstein in 1916.
options: In the 2010s, by the LIGO observatory
In the 1920s, just after their prediction
In the 1970s, thanks to the first satellites
They have never been detected before
quiz.question: In what decade were gravitational waves predicted by Einstein in 1916 first detected?
